To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
students who transfer credit to the Open university are not a homogenous group.
credit transfer students are not a homogeneous group and the reasons they transfer credit are varied and complex.

1) students who transfer credit to the Open Unversity are more likely to be mature, part-time, female students who have studied previously and are more likely to have a clear idea of their career plans; 2) students who transfer from other HE institutions are more likely to transfer a larger number of credits and to transfer from a range of subjects than students who transfer from FE; 3) students who transfer credits from FE to the Open University are more likely to study a single subject
In summary, our research is concerned with

how credit transfer can be used to facilitate the movement between higher education institutions, to enable students to re-engage with higher education, to facilitate lifelong learning and to support the development of students’ future career aspirations.
understanding how credit transfer serves the different constituencies of the Open University student body.
the ways in which credit transfer is experienced by different groups of students and how these experiences are shaped by the different disciplinary contexts within which students are studying.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the transfer of credit is not a simple or straightforward process and that credit transfer does not necessarily serve all students in the same way.
the students who are transferring credit to the OU are doing so in order to achieve a specific goal, but this goal is different in each of the disciplines.
credit transfer is a mechanism that serves the interests of students who have a clear sense of their academic goals.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
credit transfer is not a one-size-fits-all mechanism for reducing wastages and that the needs of credit transfer students should be understood within their own disciplinary and personal contexts.
credit transfer is a complex process that is not always about wastage and drop out.
credit transfer is a mechanism for re-engaging with study, but the reasons and outcomes of credit transfer are not uniform across all groups of students.
The main takeaway from our work is that
credit transfer is not a one-size-fits-all mechanism, but rather that it serves different constituencies and that it is important to understand how it is used by different groups of students.
credit transfer students are a diverse group and the motivations for their re-engagement are complex.

credit transfer is a diverse phenomenon and is used by a wide range of students in ways that are not necessarily connected to the policy objectives of reducing wastage or increasing lifelong learning.
